In-Distribution Steering: Balancing Control and Coherence in Language Model Generation

Abstract

Activation steering methods control large language model (LLM) behavior by modifying internal activations at inference time. However, most existing activation steering methods rely on a fixed steering strength, leading to either insufficient control or unadapted intervention that degrades text plausibility and coherence. We introduce In-Distribution Steering (IDS), a novel method that adapts steering strength based on the input data distribution in representation space. IDS dynamically adjusts interventions according to how far a given input lies within the distribution, enabling adaptive intervention and generation stability during text generation. Experiments demonstrate that IDS achieves strong accuracy on classification tasks while producing coherent text without collapse, making IDS particularly well suited for real-world applications.

Keywords: Alignment, steering, safety, interpretability

Arthur Vogels1, Benjamin Wong1, Yann Choho1, Annabelle Blangero1, Milan Bhan1,2

Abstract content

1.  Introduction

Despite their remarkable generalization capabilities, autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) can behave in undesirable ways. LLMs may produce factual inaccuracies Huang et al. (2025), behave unsafely Bengio et al. (2025) or be misaligned Shen et al. (2023). These problems arise because LLMs learn their objectives from broad web-scale data Weber et al. (2024), which rarely aligns perfectly with the specific requirements of any particular application. As LLMs are increasingly integrated into high-stakes or user-facing applications, it becomes essential to ensure their reliability, safety, and controllability without sacrificing fluency or creativity Wang et al. (2024).

Several approaches have been proposed to control LLM behavior. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is widely used to align models with human preferences  Christiano et al. (2017); Bai et al. (2022), but it has significant drawbacks: it requires large amounts of data and computing power, and it modifies LLMs internal weights in ways that are difficult to interpret. This opaque modification process can introduce new biases or harm the model’s performance on unrelated tasks Sharma et al. (2023). Prompt engineering Marvin et al. (2023) offers a lighter and more flexible alternative, but its effects are indirect and highly sensitive to context.

Activation steering Rimsky et al. (2024) offers a compelling alternative to RLHF and prompt engineering. Activation steering operates directly on LLMs internal activations during inference, modifying them along learned directions called steering vectors. Grounded in the linear representation hypothesis Mikolov et al. (2013); Elhage et al. (2022); Park et al. (2024), steering vectors represent directions in the LLMs representation space that corresponds to high-level concepts Bhan et al. (2025b) or behaviors, such as truthfulness Li et al. (2024), refusal Arditi et al. (2024), deceptiveness Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) or faithfulness Bhan et al. (2025a). By moving activations along such a vector, the LLM can be steered toward a specific behavior without changing its parameters, making activation steering a transparent and low-cost option for LLM control Turner et al. (2024); Rimsky et al. (2024). Several approaches have been proposed to compute and apply steering vectors in practice Rimsky et al. (2024); Turner et al. (2024); Hedström et al. (2025). However, (1) they rely on a fixed steering strength leading to either over or under steering Rimsky et al. (2024); Turner et al. (2024), (2) they are not extensively tested on open-ended text generation Hedström et al. (2025) an (3) they do not aim to generate plausible steered text Rimsky et al. (2024); Hedström et al. (2025).

To overcome these limitations, we introduce In-distribution Steering (IDS), an activation steering method that dynamically adjusts steering intensity to efficiently reach a specific behavior while staying plausible during open-ended text generation. Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce IDS, a novel activation steering approach method for dynamically adjusting steering strength on a per-input basis, enabling precise behavioral control while maintaining the plausibility and coherence of generated text.

  • •

    We evaluate IDS across six LLMs and seven datasets, and compare its performance with two competitors, providing strong evidence of its effectiveness, robustness, and generality on single token prediction and open-ended text generation.

  • •

    We run an ablation study of IDS performance, shedding light on the mechanisms underlying its success.

This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents how existing approaches perform activation steering. Section 3 introduce IDS. In Sections 4, run our experiments to compare IDS to competitors. As shown in Figure 1, IDS leads to the best compromise between steering performance (high SPI) and text plausibility (low perplexity), being along the Pareto Frontier.

2.  Background and Related Work

This section first introduces the linear representation hypothesis, which motivates the use of steering vectors. We then describe techniques for computing steering vectors from model activations. Finally, we formalize activation steering that our method builds upon.

2.1.  Background

Linear Representation Hypothesis.

The linear representation hypothesis states that high-level concepts and behavioral properties in neural networks can be encoded as directions in activation space Mikolov et al. (2013); Elhage et al. (2022); Park et al. (2024). Under this hypothesis, a model’s internal representations can be decomposed into interpretable linear components, where each direction corresponds to a semantic or behavioral feature. This geometric perspective suggests that moving activations along specific directions can induce predictable changes in model behavior without retraining or fine-tuning the model Turner et al. (2024); Rimsky et al. (2024). Empirical evidence across various architectures supports this view, demonstrating that semantic properties like truthfulness and refusal align with learnable linear directions in representation space Marks and Tegmark (2024); Arditi et al. (2024). In the following, we call these behavioral linear representations steering vectors.

Steering Vectors Computation.

Given the linear representation hypothesis, several methods have been proposed to identify which directions in activation space correspond to desired behavioral properties. The most widely used approach is the difference of means (diff-mean) method, which relies on constructing contrastive datasets pairs of examples differing in a target property (e.g., toxic vs. non-toxic, refusal vs. non-refusal) and computing the average difference in their internal activations Zou et al. (2023a); Rimsky et al. (2024). This yields a steering vector that captures the direction separating the two behaviors in representation space. Beyond diff-mean, several works have proposed supervised probing techniques, where linear classifiers such as logistic regression or support vector machines (SVMs) are trained to separate latent representations associated with different behaviors Alain and Bengio (2018); Li et al. (2024). Steering vectors are derived from these learned classifiers as the normal vectors of the decision boundaries, effectively encoding a given behavior.

Activation Steering.

Having established how steering vectors are computed, we now formalize how they are applied to modify model behavior. Activation steering refers to techniques that guide a language model’s behavior by directly modifying its internal activations during inference Rimsky et al. (2024). As the model processes input text, it computes intermediate representations at each layer encoding semantic and behavioral information that can be manipulated to control the model’s outputs. Formally, activation steering applies the following intervention at specific layers and token positions:

𝐡l,p←𝐡l,p+αl,p​𝐯l.\mathbf{h}_{l,p}\leftarrow\mathbf{h}_{l,p}+\alpha_{l,p}\mathbf{v}_{l}. (1)

where 𝐡l,p∈ℝd\mathbf{h}_{l,p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} represents the original activation at layer l∈Ll\in L and token position p∈Tp\in T. Steering is performed by adding a steering vector 𝐯l∈ℝd\mathbf{v}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} which encodes the desired behavioral direction at layer ll, while the coefficient αl,p∈ℝ\alpha_{l,p}\in\mathbb{R} controls the intervention strength at that specific layer and token position. This additive intervention shifts the model’s internal representations toward target properties without modifying model parameters.

2.2.  Related Work

Rimsky et al. (2024) introduce Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), an activation-steering technique based on steering vectors obtained with diff-mean. The authors demonstrate that CAA can reliably guide the model toward specific behaviors in both multiple-choice and open-generation settings. To evaluate performance, they report behavioral metrics such as accuracy on contrastive question-answering benchmarks and GPT-4 preference ratings for open-ended generations. A key limitation of CAA is its use of a fixed steering factor across all prompts and token positions (αl,p=α\alpha_{l,p}=\alpha following Equation 1). This uniform steering factor can cause understeering or oversteering depending on the input text. Weaker-than-necessary interventions may fail to achieve the desired effect, whereas too strong interventions may push activations outside the natural distribution of the target behavior, increasing the risk of collapse and non plausibility during text generation.

More recently, Hedström et al. (2025) proposed an approach based on steering vectors obtained with linear probes, called Mechanistic Error Reduction with Abstention (MERA). In this method, a calibration threshold is defined to determine when to apply steering, and the steering strength is computed using a closed-form solution. The steering strength scales proportionally with the predicted error of the linear probes. Steering is applied only when the probe’s prediction exceeds the calibrated threshold; otherwise, the model abstains from intervention. MERA consistently outperforms several steering baselines such as CAA, achieving notable accuracy gains. However, MERA is primarily designed for supervised tasks and does not directly address open-ended text generation. Its evaluation does not include text plausibility metrics.

3.  Proposed Approach: In-distribution Steering

This section introduces the core principles of In-distribution Steering (IDS), our proposed activation steering approach. IDS aims at determining the optimal value of the steering factors at each layer and token position by leveraging the distributions of activations obtained from a dataset of prompts exhibiting the target behavior. Following Equation 1, the objective is to determine the optimal value of αpl\alpha^{l}_{p} such that the steered activation remains consistent with the distribution of activations at layer ll corresponding to prompts that exhibit the desired behavior, denoted by 𝒟l+\mathcal{D}^{+}_{l}. Our method proceeds in three stages:

  1. 1.

    Distributions Modeling. We construct a contrastive dataset to characterize the distributions of activations for the positive (aligned behavior) and negative (unaligned behavior) classes, and we define a threshold on a distance measure that determines whether an activation lies within the target distribution.

  2. 2.

    Optimal Steering Factor Determination. We formulate the determination of the steering factor as a constrained optimization problem, where the objective is to apply the strongest possible steering while ensuring that activations remain in-distribution. A closed-form solution is derived to allow efficient computation.

  3. 3.

    Layers Selection. We restrict interventions to layers that are discriminative for the target behavior, using a threshold on a F1-score as indictor of the discriminative power of a layer.

3.1.  Distributions Modeling

Contrastive Dataset Creation

The first step of our approach consists in modeling two distributions using a contrastive dataset. We model the distribution of the activations at the last token position for prompts in which the target behavior is either present (positive) or absent (negative). Formally, for a given layer ll, we define the corresponding distributions as

𝒟l−=𝒟⁡(𝐡l,−1−)𝒟l+=𝒟⁡(𝐡l,−1+),\mathcal{D}^{-}_{l}=\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{h}^{-}_{l,-1})\quad\quad\mathcal{D}^{+}_{l}=\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{h}^{+}_{l,-1}),

where 𝐡l,ps\mathbf{h}^{s}_{l,p} denotes the activations at token position pp and layer ll for prompts in which the behavior is absent (s=−s=-) or present (s=+s=+).

In the context of multiple-choice questions (MCQs), some existing methods construct contrastive datasets by completing the same prompt with an answer token that either reveals or does not reveal the expected answer. Activations are then collected at the first answer token position as in  Rimsky et al. (2024). While this approach makes more efficient use of the data, since each prompt produces a contrastive pair, the resulting activations are collected at the answer token. Their distribution may differ from that of the prompt tokens. For this reason, we instead construct our datasets by separating prompts where the model naturally exhibits the expected behavior from those where it does not, thereby allowing us to compute the relevant distributions directly on the prompt activations. Steering vectors are then computed for each layer ll from the difference in means between the two distributions as follows:

𝐯l=1|D+|​∑𝐡l,−1+−1|D−|​∑𝐡l,−1−\mathbf{v}_{l}=\dfrac{1}{|D^{+}|}\sum\mathbf{h}^{+}_{l,-1}-\dfrac{1}{|D^{-}|}\sum\mathbf{h}^{-}_{l,-1} (2)

Reducing dimension with PCA

Since the activations lie in a high-dimensional space, directly modeling the distributions is problematic due to the curse of dimensionality Peng et al. (2023). In such settings, distances become less informative and density estimation requires prohibitively many samples. To address this, we first apply a PCA to the union of the two datasets, 𝐡l,−1−∪𝐡l,−1+\mathbf{h}^{-}_{l,-1}\cup\mathbf{h}^{+}_{l,-1}, to obtain a lower-dimensional projection of the data. We argue that the separability between the two classes will be preserved in the reduced space if the between-class variance, induced by the presence or absence of the behavior, dominates within-class variance Teo et al. (2025). This way, we ensure that the subsequent modeling steps remain sensitive to interventions in the direction of steering.

Modeling Distances with Mahalanobis

The next step consists in modeling the distance of an activation to the distributions 𝒟lpca-\mathcal{D}^{\text{pca-}}_{l} and 𝒟lpca+\mathcal{D}^{\text{pca+}}_{l} in the reduced space. For this purpose, we employ the Mahalanobis distance, which explicitly accounts for variability along different directions. This choice is further motivated by the expectation that within-distribution variability will be limited along the concept direction. In contrast, alternative measures such as the Euclidean distance fail to capture this heterogeneity, as they treat all directions as equally informative.

Once the distances are modeled, we define a threshold of the form ϵ=d0.95\epsilon=d_{0.95}, where d0.95d_{0.95} denotes the 95th-percentile of the distance distribution. The choice of the 95th-percentile threshold parallels the use of a significance level of α=0.05\alpha=0.05 in hypothesis testing. This threshold provides a general criterion to determine whether a given activation is considered in-distribution (if the distance lies below the threshold) or out-of-distribution (if it lies above).

Optimization Problem

Following Equation 1, we define the steering factor αl,p\alpha_{l,p} at layer ll and token position pp as the largest value such that the steered activation remains consistent with the distribution of the target class. Concretely, if we want to steer an example from the negative to the positive class, the problem can be formulated as:

αl,p\displaystyle{\alpha_{l,p}} =maxα,\displaystyle=\max\quad\alpha, (3)
s.t.dM+l​(P​C​A​(𝐡l,p+α​𝐯l))2≤ϵl2\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad d_{M^{+}}^{l}\big(PCA(\mathbf{h}_{l,p}+\alpha\mathbf{v}_{l})\big)^{2}\leq\epsilon_{l}^{2}

3.3.  Layers Selection

In the third step, after determining the optimal value of the steering factors, we introduce mechanisms to insure that the interventions are performed on layers with high discriminative power, while ensuring that the propagation of these interventions across layers stays in-distribution.

Steering Layer Selection Based on F1-Score Performance

To assess whether an intervention should be applied at layer ll for a given behavior, we evaluate the discriminative power of the corresponding steering vector 𝐯l\mathbf{v}^{l} using the F1-score. Specifically, once a steering vector is computed, it is employed as a classifier on the dataset from which it was derived, and the resulting F1-score is recorded. We then impose a threshold of 0.7 on this metric: an intervention at layer ll will be performed during steering only if the associated F1-score exceeds this threshold. Performance metrics for other values of this F1-score threshold are presented in Section 4.2.

4.  Experimental Settings

4.1.  Experimental Protocol

Datasets and Models.

We conduct experiments in a single-logit generation setting on supervised classification tasks: SMS Spam Filtering (sms) Almeida et al. (2011) and MMLU Hendrycks et al. (2020). We further evaluate on multi-choice instruction following across five key AI safety behaviors from Rimsky et al. (2024): coordination with other AIs (coordinate-other-ais), corrigibility (corrigible-neutral-HHH), hallucination, refusal, and myopic reward. Finally, we test our method in open-ended text generation using a combination of harmful instructions from diverse datasets Zou et al. (2023b); Huang et al. (2023); Mazeika et al. (2023); Mazeika et al. (2024), paired with harmless instructions sampled from Alpaca Dubois et al. (2023), following the setup of Arditi et al. (2024). We also reuse two datasets of Rimsky et al. (2024) in an open-ended setting to further show the versatility of our method. We distinguish the dataset refusal for single logit generation (refusal) and open-ended generation (refusalog).

We apply IDS and its competitors to steer 6 decoder-only models. The library used to import these models is tranformers, with the following backbones: gemma-2-2B-it, gemma-2-9B-it, qwen-2.5-1.5B-it, qwen-2.5-7B-it, Llama-3.2-9B-it, Llama-3.1-8B-it.

Competitors.

We compare IDS to three competitors. We first run CAA by computing a steering vector as diff-mean based on the contrastive dataset of interest. The steering vector is computed from the last token position in the prompt for each layer. CAA is tested by setting the steering factors to 1 and 1.5, respectively denoted as CAA-1 and CAA-1.5. We also compare our approach to MERA, by setting the steering factor as αl,p=max⁡(0,λ−𝐯l⊤​𝐡l,p‖𝐯l‖22)\alpha_{l,p}=\mathrm{max}\left(0,\frac{\lambda-\mathbf{v}_{l}^{\top}\mathbf{h}_{l,p}}{||\mathbf{v}_{l}||_{2}^{2}}\right), where λ\lambda is an hyperparameter calibrated on the SMS dataset. Both MERA and IDS method are agnostic to the choice of steering vector. We adopt the diff-mean steering vector due to its simplicity and suitability for both single-logit and open-ended generation settings.

Metrics.

We measure the impact of steering on aligning previously non-aligned answers. The definition of a non-aligned answer depends on the task: incorrect predictions in classification tasks, or responses failing to exhibit the desired behavior in multi-choice instruction following and open-ended text generation tasks. Following Hedström et al. (2025), we evaluate steering methods using the Steering Performance Impact (SPI), which quantifies the proportion of unaligned answers corrected by steering when positive, and the proportion of aligned answers wrongfully changed when negative:

SPI={A¯−A1−A,if ​A¯>A,A¯−AA,otherwise,\mathrm{SPI}=\begin{cases}\frac{\bar{A}-A}{1-A},&\text{if }\bar{A}>A,\\[6.0pt] \frac{\bar{A}-A}{A},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (9)

where A¯\bar{A} (resp. AA) denotes the proportion of aligned answers with (resp. without) steering. In the open-generation setting, we evaluate both alignment success and model confidence. We rely on GPT-4.1 to automatically assess the proportion of generations that exhibit the targeted behaviors. We also compute perplexity (PPL) to evaluate the text plausibility.

4.2.  Experimental Results

Global Results.

IDS is evaluated using the same set of hyperparameters accross all experiments: ϵ=d0.95\epsilon=d_{0.95}, threshold on F1-score =0.7=0.7 and Proportion of variance explained =40%=40\%. We first report the performance of the different methods presented on the single-logit and open-ended text generation tasks. Table 1 shows the experimental results obtained by IDS and its competitors on all the analyzed datasets and models for non open-ended generation (single-logit). The results demonstrate that IDS achieves superior SPI performance across diverse evaluation benchmarks, obtaining the best average rank of 1.67 across all datasets and model sizes. Notably, IDS ranks first on average for 5 out of 6 models, with only Llama-3.1-8B showing a slight preference for MERA (0.34 vs 0.29). IDS also ranks first on average for 5 out of 7 datasets. This demonstrates that IDS generalizes effectively across different model architectures and datasets. Beyond ranking first, IDS achieves substantially higher absolute performance scores compared to baselines. Most notably, IDS outperforms MERA by considerable margins on several models (up to 18 points difference).

Table 2 shows the experimental results obtained by IDS and its competitors on open-ended generation tasks. Again, IDS achieves the best steering performance while maintaining correct generation quality, ranking first overall with an average SPI rank of 1.39. IDS ranks first on average SPI for all 6 models and 4 datasets. Moreover, for each individual dataset-model combination, IDS consistently ranks either first or second in SPI, never falling below second place across all 18 configurations. This consistency underscores the robustness and reliability of our approach across diverse scenarios. IDS ranks third in average perplexity, but get a perplexity close to CAA-1.5 and CAA-1 on average, whereas MERA generates non plausible text with very high perplexity. If CAA methods produce the most plausible text with the lowest perplexity, it fails dramatically in steering effectiveness with poor average SPI ranks (3.00 and 2.83) and weak absolute performance. This way, while IDS does not achieve the lowest perplexity, it avoids instabilities and maintains consistent generation quality across all scenarios, suggesting the best trade-off between steering effectiveness (SPI) and text plausibility (PPL). The results shown in Table 1 and 2 are summarized and aggregated at the model level in Figure 1, showing that IDS is along the Pareto frontier between steering performance and text plausibility.

Linking Over-steering and Collapse.

Results in Table 2 show that collapse (high perplexity and low SPI) can occur on text generated with MERA steering, notably on the Refusal dataset with gemma-2-2B. We argue that these results are provoked by larger values of the steering factors in average. Table 3 shows average steering factors aggregated over layers and token positions for the 3 open-ended generation datasets for IDS, MERA and CAA-1 on gemma-2-2B. The steering factor is higher on average with MERA on the refusal and hallucination datasets, where MERA tends to generate highly non-plausible text. Figure 3 and 4 respectively show the difference in the propagation of the steering factors for a prompt that collapse with MERA and not with IDS. The objective is to make the gemma-2-2B answer to a problematic prompt ("I want to get high on prescription amphetamines. What symptoms should I say I ´m having when I talk to my doctor?") The intensity of the steering factors remains larger through the successive layers of the model, questioning the adaptability of the calibration of such approach. In single-logit generation tasks, larger steering factors are generally acceptable, as the risk of instability from repeated interventions at the token level is limited. However, in open-ended text generation, such strong and cumulative interventions can drive the activations out of distribution, ultimately leading to collapse and non-plausible text.

Ablation Study.

We conduct an ablation study of IDS on Gemma-2-2B across 5 datasets, varying three key hyperparameters: (1) the proportion of explained variance retained during PCA, (2) the Mahalanobis distance threshold (ϵ\epsilon) for distribution assessment, and (3) the F1 score threshold for triggering activation steering.

Figure 5 shows the average SPI with standard deviation across quartiles of explained variance for PCA. Retaining between 30% and 42% of the variance yields the highest and most stable SPI results across datasets. This finding aligns with expectations: retaining too much variance results in high-dimensional projections where distribution assessment becomes unreliable due to the curse of dimensionality. Figure 6 reveals a slight positive relationship between the Mahalanobis distance threshold and steering performance, suggesting that allowing slightly more distributional deviation can improve steering effectiveness. Figure 7 demonstrates that steering performance begins to decline beyond an F1 score threshold of approximately 80%. This behavior is expected: excessively restrictive F1 thresholds dramatically reduce the number of instances where steering is applied, thereby diminishing overall steering effectiveness. We show similar results with gemma-2-9B in Appendix 8.5.

5.  Discussion

This paper focused on directional steering by moving along a steering vector in the representation space. Recent work has shown that rotating activations in the representation space (angular steering) can outperform unidirectional steering Vu and Nguyen (2025). However, that work does not guarantee that angular steering interventions remain within the data distribution. Extending our approach to angular steering represents a promising direction for future improvement. We also plan to apply IDS to generate more truthful rationales when answering questions that require complex reasoning. This could enhance the performance of recently proposed methods that answer questions in an explain-then-predict fashion Bhan et al. (2024); Wei et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2023); Yao et al. (2024). Additionally, applying steering during the inference of reasoning models Feng et al. (2025) could lead to improved performance on complex tasks.

6.  Conclusion

This work introduces IDS, an activation steering methods addressing the fundamental challenge of balancing behavioral control and text coherence in language model text generation. By dynamically adjusting intervention strength based on the input’s position within the target behavior’s activation distribution, IDS prevents over and under-steering.

Our experimental evaluation across six language models and seven datasets demonstrates IDS’s superior performance compared to established competitors including CAA and MERA, with consistently optimal Steering Performance Impact (SPI) scores while maintaining text plausibility (perplexity). IDS theoretical basis, i.e. modeling activation distributions using PCA and Mahalanobis distance measures, provides a sound approach with a closed-form solution that enables efficient real-time computation.

IDS enables fine-grained control over LLM behavior while maintaining output quality, making it valuable for both alignment research and practical deployment. It allows stronger safety interventions without losing coherence and adapts in real time to diverse inputs. This positions IDS as a practical tool for deploying more controllable and reliable language models in high-stakes applications.

8.  Appendix

8.1.  Scientific Libraries

We used several open-source libraries in this work: pytorch Paszke et al. (2019), HuggingFace transformers Wolf et al. (2020), transformer-lens.

8.2.  Autoregressive Language Models Implementation Details

Language Models.

The library used to import the pretrained autoregressive language models is Hugging-Face. In particular, the backbone version of the model used in the article are as follows: gemma-2-2B-it, gemma-2-9B-it, qwen-2.5-1.5B-it, qwen-2.5-7B-it, Llama-3.2-9B-it, Llama-3.1-8B-it.

Text Generation.

Text generation was performed using the native functions of the TransformerLens library: generate. In the open-ended text generation setting, we sample up to 150 tokens. Greedy decoding is used for sake of reproducibility of the results.

8.3.  Closed-Form Solution

Closed-Form Solution in the Euclidean Case

If we simplify the problem by replacing the Mahalanobis distance with the Euclidean distance to the center of the target distribution in the original space, the optimization becomes considerably easier. Let 𝝁+\boldsymbol{\mu}^{+} denote the mean of the positive-class distribution. The problem reduces to:

α∗=maxα,\displaystyle\alpha^{*}=\max\quad\alpha, (10)
s.t.‖𝐡+α​𝐯−𝝁+‖2<ϵ2.\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad\|\mathbf{h}+\alpha\mathbf{v}-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{+}\|^{2}<\epsilon^{2}. (11)

This is a convex quadratic constraint, equivalent to solving for the largest feasible root of the polynomial

f⁡(α)=a​α2+b​α+c,f(\alpha)=a\alpha^{2}+b\alpha+c, (12)

with coefficients

a=‖𝐯‖2,b=2​𝐯⊤​(𝐡−𝝁+),c=‖𝐡−𝝁+‖2−ϵ2.a=\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2},\quad b=2\mathbf{v}^{\top}(\mathbf{h}-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{+}),\quad c=\|\mathbf{h}-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{+}\|^{2}-\epsilon^{2}.

The closed-form solution is obtained from the quadratic formula:

α1,2=−b±b2−4​a​c2​a.\alpha_{1,2}=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}.

Depending on the discriminant Δ=b2−4​a​c\Delta=b^{2}-4ac, three cases arise:

  • •

    If Δ>0\Delta>0, there are two real roots. The feasible region corresponds to the interval between the two roots, and α∗\alpha^{*} is the larger root.

  • •

    If Δ=0\Delta=0, there is one real root, which corresponds to the unique feasible solution.

  • •

    If Δ<0\Delta<0, there is no feasible solution that places 𝐡′\mathbf{h^{\prime}} strictly inside the distribution. In this case, we take

    α∗=−b2​a,\alpha^{*}=-\frac{b}{2a},

    which minimizes the distance to the target distribution.

Extension to Mahalanobis Distance in PCA Space

When using the Mahalanobis distance in the PCA-reduced space, the problem remains conceptually equivalent to the Euclidean case, provided we account for the linear transformations induced by PCA and covariance normalization.

Let the target distribution 𝒟+\mathcal{D}^{+} be characterized by mean 𝝁+\boldsymbol{\mu}^{+} and positive definite covariance matrix 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma}, which admits a Cholesky decomposition 𝚺=𝐋𝐋⊤\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^{\top}. The Mahalanobis distance of a point 𝐱\mathbf{x} to 𝒟+\mathcal{D}^{+} can be expressed as

M​a​h​a​(𝐱)=(𝐱−𝝁+)⊤​𝚺−1​(𝐱−𝝁+)=‖𝐋−1​(𝐱−𝝁+)‖,\begin{split}Maha(\mathbf{x})&=\sqrt{(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{+})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{+})}\\ &=\big\|\mathbf{L}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{+})\big\|,\end{split} (13)

which reduces to a Euclidean norm after applying the linear transformation 𝐋−1\mathbf{L}^{-1}.

Similarly, let PCA project a vector 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} into pca​(𝐱)∈ℝk\text{pca}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{k}, given by:

p​c​a​(𝐱)=𝐂⊤​(𝐱−𝝁),pca(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{C}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}), (14)

where 𝐂∈ℝd×k\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} contains the first kk principal components. For a steered activation 𝐡′\mathbf{h^{\prime}}, we obtain:

p​c​a​(𝐡′)=p​c​a​(𝐡+α​𝐯)=p​c​a​(𝐡)+α​𝐂⊤​𝐯.pca(\mathbf{h^{\prime}})=pca(\mathbf{h}+\alpha\mathbf{v})=pca(\mathbf{h})+\alpha\mathbf{C}^{\top}\mathbf{v}. (15)

Combining these results, the Mahalanobis constraint becomes

M​a​h​apca+​(p​c​a​(𝐡+α​𝐯))2<ϵ2\displaystyle Maha^{\text{pca+}}(pca(\mathbf{h}+\alpha\mathbf{v}))^{2}<\epsilon^{2}
⟹∥𝐋pca+−1pca(𝐡)+α𝐋pca+−1𝐂⊤𝐯−𝐋pca+−1𝝁pca+∥2<ϵ2.\displaystyle\implies\big\|\mathbf{L}_{\text{pca}}^{+^{-1}}pca(\mathbf{h})+\alpha\mathbf{L}_{\text{pca}}^{+^{-1}}\mathbf{C}^{\top}\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{L}_{\text{pca}}^{+^{-1}}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{+}_{\text{pca}}\big\|^{2}<\epsilon^{2}.

Thus, the problem reduces to the same quadratic form as in (11), with the substitutions:

𝐡→𝐋pca+−1pca(𝐡),\displaystyle\mathbf{h}\;\rightarrow\;\mathbf{L}_{\text{pca}}^{+^{-1}}pca(\mathbf{h}),
𝐯→𝐋pca+−1𝐂⊤𝐯,\displaystyle\mathbf{v}\;\rightarrow\;\mathbf{L}_{\text{pca}}^{+^{-1}}\mathbf{C}^{\top}\mathbf{v},
𝝁+→𝐋pca+−1𝝁+pca.\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}^{+}\;\rightarrow\;\mathbf{L}_{\text{pca}}^{+^{-1}}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{+}_{\text{pca}}.

This shows that the same closed-form reasoning applies in both the Euclidean and Mahalanobis settings, with only the appropriate linear transformations required.
